sections.html:
Framingham is a Middlesex County city in the MetroWest part of Greater Boston, about 25 square miles of land with 72,362 residents at the 2020 census. It was a town for more than 300 years, and voters approved a mayor and council charter in April 2017. The city form began on January 1, 2018.

After World War II the town grew quickly, and much of the housing from that period is split-level and ranch style. Sellers of those homes often deal with original kitchens, older baths and systems that have never been updated.

Framingham is split into business districts and villages, and a house in each tends to attract a different buyer.

  • Golden Triangle: the retail and office district on the east side, bordered by Route 9, Route 30 and Speen Street. TJX has its world headquarters at Route 30 and Speen Street.
  • Downtown and South Framingham: the commercial center that grew with the railroad in the 1880s.
  • West Framingham: centered on Route 9 with large office parks and most of the city's apartment and condominium complexes.
  • Framingham Centre, Saxonville and Nobscot: older villages. The Framingham Centre Common Historic District is the historic center, with Framingham State University beside it.

A house near Route 9 can draw steady rental interest and also carry heavy traffic noise. Renters, commuters and office-park employees all show up as potential occupants.

Framingham sits roughly halfway between Boston and Worcester. The Massachusetts Turnpike (Interstate 90), Route 9, Route 30, Route 126 and Route 135 all cross the city.

Access pointWhat it offers
MBTA Framingham/Worcester LineCommuter rail to South Station and Back Bay; about 42 to 45 minutes to Back Bay
Logan ExpressDirect bus to Logan Airport from the Shoppers World property off Turnpike exit 13
MetroWest Regional Transit AuthorityRegional bus routes linking Framingham with nearby towns
Logan International AirportAbout 25 miles away

Downtown is split by the rail tracks and Waverly Street (Route 135). Homes within walking range of the station draw commuters, while houses near the Turnpike and Route 9 interchanges draw buyers who want quick highway access.

Buyers with children usually ask which elementary school serves a house. Get the school assignment from the district before you list or negotiate, and have the answer ready. A wrong guess costs trust, so confirm it rather than assume. Families often decide on the school before they look at the kitchen.

Framingham bills property tax quarterly, with installments due on August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. Payments after the due date accrue interest at 14 percent per year under G.L. c. 59, s. 57C, counted from the day after the due date.

The city tries to mail bills at least 30 days before each due date. Not receiving a bill does not remove the obligation, so contact the Tax Collector if nothing arrives two or three weeks before a date. The Treasurer/Collector is at 150 Concord Street, Room 111, phone 508-532-5430.

If you sell in the middle of a billing quarter, the closing statement normally adjusts the current installment between seller and buyer. Ask your closing attorney which installments are paid and which are still open. The city explains more on its Important Tax Information page.

Selling a one or two family home requires a Fire Department smoke and carbon monoxide detector inspection before closing. Apply and pay online, then call Fire Department Administration at 508-532-5930 to schedule the visit.

  • Allow at least three weeks between the inspection request and your closing date.
  • Inspections are generally held Monday to Friday, typically in the afternoon.
  • The house number must be on the structure itself, not on a door, at least 3 inches tall and visible from the nearest street.
  • Fire Headquarters is at 10 Loring Drive.

A failed inspection is a common reason a closing slips by a few days. Replacing old alarms before you apply is usually cheaper than a second visit. The city's inspection page links the requirements sheet.

sections.h2: What Framingham sellers usually run into
sections.html:
• Mid-century houses with dated systems that need work before a conventional buyer's lender will approve them.
  • Inherited homes where the owner lives out of state and has not cleared the contents.
  • Tenant-occupied homes and multi-family properties, especially near downtown and along Route 9.
  • Open tax installments, or a closing date that has to fit around the three-week fire inspection lead time.

A cash buyer who purchases as is can skip repair lists and showings, which matters most on inherited and tenant-occupied properties. You still need a clear title, an inspection certificate and tax adjustments at closing, so line those up early.

sections.h2: How do you decide between listing and a cash sale?
sections.html:
Listing makes sense when the house is in good shape and you can wait out showings, an appraisal and a buyer's financing. A cash sale makes sense when time, condition or occupancy is the bigger problem.

Compare net amounts, not headline prices. A listing involves agent commission, repairs a lender may require and weeks of carrying costs such as tax installments and utilities. A direct sale removes several of those lines, along with the uncertainty of a buyer's financing falling through, but usually comes at a lower number. Ask any buyer for the offer in writing, and ask the closing attorney what you would actually receive after the mortgage payoff and tax adjustments.

Split-levels and ranches from the postwar years often still have the original kitchen, an older bath and a heating or electrical system that has never been replaced. A buyer's lender may want some of that fixed before it will approve a loan, which is where deals stall. You have three choices: repair before listing, offer a credit, or sell as is. Get a contractor's quote for the biggest item, usually the roof, the heating system or the panel, so you know what each choice costs. Put the quotes beside a written cash offer and a listing estimate, and the best path for your situation usually becomes clear.

Gather permit records for any additions or finished basements, since a missing permit is a question the buyer's attorney will ask.

Work backward from your closing date. At least three weeks out, file the fire inspection request. Before that, order any alarm replacements and put the house number on the structure. A few weeks earlier still, ask the Treasurer/Collector which installments are open, gather the deed and permit records, and talk to your closing attorney about the mortgage payoff. Doing these in order, with a date next to each, keeps a few days of slip from turning into a missed date.

faqs.q: Is Framingham a town or a city?
faqs.a: A city. Voters approved a mayor and council charter in April 2017, and the city form took effect on January 1, 2018.

faqs.q: Do I need a smoke and carbon monoxide inspection to sell in Framingham?
faqs.a: Yes. The Fire Department inspects the detectors for sales, and the city asks for at least three weeks of lead time before your closing date.

faqs.q: When are Framingham property tax bills due?
faqs.a: Installments are due August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. Late payments carry 14 percent annual interest.
The MBTA Framingham/Worcester Line runs to South Station and Back Bay. The trip to Back Bay takes about 42 to 45 minutes.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Framingham house that has tenants?
faqs.a: Yes, and some cash buyers purchase tenant-occupied homes as is. The lease stays in force, so ask the buyer how they handle the tenancy before you sign.
